title: India's Sugar Prices Hit Record Highs as Government Races to Cool Market Before Diwali
excerpt: New Delhi tightens stock limits and opens duty-free imports for the first time in nearly a decade as festival season demand meets a crop shortfall.
body:
• Indian wholesale sugar prices have surged over 10% in the past month to record highs, with retail prices reaching Rs 58-60 per kg in some markets.
  • The government has halved stockholding limits to 15 days for bulk consumers and approved 1 million tonnes of duty-free imports until October 31.
  • Patchy rainfall and crop diseases reduced sugar production below annual consumption, leaving mill inventories at their lowest in over three decades.
  • Industry officials say the price surge is partly driven by speculative buying ahead of the festival season, not just a structural shortage.

Record Prices Trigger Government Action

India's sugar market is under unprecedented pressure as prices have surged to record highs ahead of the country's peak festival season, prompting a battery of government interventions not seen in nearly a decade.

Wholesale sugar prices in Kolhapur, a key trading hub in Maharashtra, jumped nearly 10.2% over the past month to Rs 4,716 per 100 kg, according to Reuters. Retail prices have climbed even higher, reaching Rs 58-60 per kg in select domestic markets. Average retail prices were up 13% year-on-year to Rs 52.30 per kg as of August 18, according to Consumer Affairs Ministry data reported by Outlook Business.

In response, the government on August 20 ordered that no dealer using more than 10 metric tonnes of sugar per month may hold inventories for longer than 15 days, down from a previous 30-day limit imposed last month. The restriction takes effect September 1 and runs through November 30, covering the entire festival season.

Duty-Free Imports Return After Nearly a Decade

In a more dramatic step, India last week approved 1 million tonnes of duty-free raw sugar imports until October 31 — the first such move in almost a decade for the world's biggest sugar consumer.

However, the market's reaction has already muted the import opportunity. Domestic prices fell nearly 20% from their record peak following the announcement, according to Reuters, eroding the profit margin for importers.

"Imports looked attractive last week, when prices were firm and rising. But the sharp price drop since the announcement has taken the shine off imports for millers."

— Rahil Shaikh, Managing Director, MEIR Commodities India

Industry sources told Reuters that imports are unlikely to exceed 500,000 tonnes — half the approved quota. Meanwhile, Indian refiners are redirecting approximately 350,000 tonnes of export-bound sugar to the domestic market, a move that could provide relief within a week, according to Bloomberg.

What's Behind the Shortage

The supply crunch stems from a combination of weather disruptions and rising ethanol diversion. Patchy rains and dry weather damaged the water-intensive sugarcane crop, while red rot and varietal problems hit production in Uttar Pradesh, a major growing state. Maharashtra saw higher crush rates but overall national production fell short of annual consumption.

Sugar inventories held by mills at the start of the new season on October 1 are expected to fall to approximately 3.5 million tonnes — the lowest level in more than three decades, Reuters reported. Mills exported about 800,000 tonnes of sugar during the current season, further reducing the domestic buffer.

The Indian Sugar Mills Association has pushed back against shortage narratives. "India does not have a sugar shortage. Our production and stock position remains fundamentally comfortable," said ISMA president Niraj Shirgaokar. He characterized the price spike as driven primarily by speculative buying and festival-season sentiment rather than a structural supply problem.

Festival Season Adds Urgency

Sugar is politically sensitive in India, where traditional sweets are central to celebrations and poorer households depend on it as an affordable source of calories. Demand typically surges from August through November as the country celebrates Ganesh Chaturthi, Dussehra, and Diwali, with bulk consumers like biscuit and confectionery makers building inventories ahead of the season.

For the Indian diaspora, the price surge is a reminder of how deeply food inflation can affect family budgets back home. NRI families sending remittances or planning trips home during the festival season will find sweet-making ingredients costlier than at any point in recent memory.

What's Next

Domestic supplies are expected to improve from mid-October when mills begin crushing the new-season crop. The government will verify compliance with stock limits using GST returns. Until the new crop arrives, the market must rely on current-season production, redirected export stocks, and whatever imports materialize before the quota window closes on October 31.
